analyses.title: Get Your Vitamin C! Robust Fact Verification with Contrastive Evidence
analyses.research_question: Can fact-verification models be made more sensitive and robust to factual changes in evolving evidence by training on contrastive revisions where small textual edits alter a claim's truth status?
analyses.methodology: The authors mine successive revisions of English Wikipedia, use a classifier to preselect likely substantive edits, and have annotators identify factual revisions and construct symmetric claims whose support status changes across versions. They augment these naturally occurring revisions with synthetic revisions derived from FEVER, producing contrastive claim-evidence examples. They train and evaluate transformer models on factual-revision flagging, support/refute/NEI fact verification, word-level rationale prediction, and factually consistent text generation. Evaluation includes VitaminC, FEVER, adversarial fact-verification and NLI datasets, contrast sensitivity, token-level rationale metrics, and generation metrics with manual checks.

key_findings.finding: An ALBERT model using the full before-and-after sentences achieved 83.18 F1 and 91.97 AUC for factual-revision flagging, outperforming edit-distance, bag-of-words, and edited-span-only baselines.

Contrastive training substantially increased sensitivity to changed evidence: the ALBERT-base FEVER-only model flipped its verdict on 55.53% of contrastive cases, whereas VitaminC plus FEVER training reached 85.89%, and the corresponding ALBERT-xlarge model reached 90.94%.

Adding VitaminC training improved performance on adversarial evaluations while largely preserving in-domain FEVER or MNLI accuracy, indicating that revision-aware examples reduced reliance on static or lexical shortcuts.
Distant token-level supervision derived from revision edits raised word-level rationale F1 from 37.33 to 47.36 and edit-prediction F1 from 31.23 to 59.11.

For factually consistent generation, the BART claim generator received an 85.83 verifier score and the BART revision generator received 76.26, with manual evaluation additionally checking grammaticality and support.

limitations: The empirical domain is English Wikipedia rather than workplace or operational communication.
Fact verification assumes an oracle retriever, so the experiments do not evaluate end-to-end discovery of corroborating evidence.

The longitudinal relation model is primarily whether an edit changes support/refute/NEI status; it does not distinguish supersession, correction, supplementation, reopening, or work-item conflict as separate relation labels.
Candidate revisions were preselected from a much larger revision pool using a learned factual-change classifier before human annotation, so the corpus reflects that selection process.
The paper does not model the distinction between a participant claiming that a task is complete and independent evidence corroborating that completion.
raw_claims: The dataset is built around factual changes between successive versions of Wikipedia sentences.
Annotators examined 304,671 revised sentences and identified 107,056 as factual modifications.
The natural revision process yielded 325,724 claim-evidence pairs, with another 163,180 pairs produced synthetically.
A factual revision is operationalized as an edit capable of changing a claim's verification label.
Full sentence context performs better than edit magnitude or edited tokens alone for factual-revision detection.
Models trained only on conventional fact-verification data frequently fail to reverse their prediction when evidence changes subtly.
Revision-derived token supervision improves identification of evidence spans that determine a verdict.
The before-and-after structure can also supervise generation of claims or sentences consistent with updated facts.

analyses.title: ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents
analyses.research_question: Can factuality verification for multi-source MCP agents explicitly preserve source ownership so that unsupported claims, contradictions, and claims supported by the wrong source are reliably blocked?
analyses.methodology: ProvenanceGuard captures MCP traces containing stable tool IDs, source IDs, and raw outputs, decomposes generated answers into atomic claims, routes each claim to source-specific evidence, and applies NLI plus evidence-derived features to determine support. It separately checks whether the source stated or implied by an answer agrees with the source to which supporting evidence was routed, allowing cross-source conflation to be detected even when pooled evidence supports the factual content. The system is evaluated on 281 medical-domain MCP-agent traces, a held-out claim set, a harder multi-source adjudicated benchmark, controlled attribution-swap probes, and repair-and-reverification experiments. The main operational metrics include reject/block F1, exact verdict accuracy, source accuracy, source-plus-relation accuracy, and repair outcomes.

key_findings.finding: On the held-out set of 40 traces and 361 claims, ProvenanceGuard achieved 0.802 reject/block F1, 0.993 reject recall, and 0.858 source accuracy over source-eligible claims.

Source-blind support baselines remained competitive on binary rejection, with MiniCheck reaching 0.783 F1, and the 0.019 F1 gap to ProvenanceGuard was not statistically significant; the distinctive measured capability was explicit claim-to-source attribution.
key_findings.section: V.4 RQ3: Comparison With Source-Blind Baselines

key_findings.finding: On the harder multi-source benchmark, reject/block F1 remained 0.846 while source accuracy fell to 0.503 and source-plus-relation accuracy to 0.229, showing that exact provenance attribution becomes much harder among semantically similar candidate sources.
key_findings.section: V.2 Multi-Source Benchmark Rerun and Multi-Tool Stress Slices

key_findings.finding: All 50 deliberately injected source-attribution swaps in the controlled conflation probes were blocked and labeled as conflations, and no repaired output retained the deliberately wrong attribution.

The repair loop made all 173 initially blocked full-trace answers pass reverification, but 144 resolutions used terminal fallback text, so verifier passage did not usually imply successful recovery of a rich substantive answer.
key_findings.section: V.5 RQ4: Repair After Source-Aware Blocking

key_findings.finding: The experiments directly demonstrate that factual support and provenance attribution are separable: a statement can be supported somewhere in the trace while still being invalid for the source to which the answer attributes it.
key_findings.section: III.6 Attribution and Conflation; V.6 RQ5

limitations: The primary empirical setting is one medical MCP-agent stack rather than longitudinal workplace or operational communication.
The main held-out evaluation contains only 40 traces, and the reported confidence intervals for several metrics are correspondingly wide.

Training and validation adjudication relies substantially on LLM-assisted labels; the paper reports human expert review of all 361 held-out claims but does not claim equivalent expert review of all training and validation labels.
The 50 source-conflation probes each contain a clear deliberate attribution swap and are not an adversarial test of arbitrary source confusion.
Repair is scored using the same verifier that triggered blocking, so successful reverification is not independent domain-level corroboration of answer completeness.
The system does not label longitudinal work-item relations such as supersession, correction, supplementation, reopening, or temporal conflict.
The public paper-artifact repository states that reproducible code and data are not currently released.
raw_claims: The verifier preserves source identity instead of pooling all tool evidence into one undifferentiated context.
Its operational reject class includes unsupported, contradicted, not-enough-evidence, and conflation cases.
A claim may be factually supported by one MCP source while being wrongly attributed to another.
The held-out evaluation contains 361 claims from 40 captured agent traces.
Exact source selection is substantially harder when many semantically close source candidates are present.
The support-only advantage over the strongest source-blind comparator is small and not statistically significant in the held-out sample.
Controlled source-attribution swaps are detected by comparing answer attribution with routed supporting evidence.
Passing the post-repair verifier does not independently prove that the repaired answer is complete or useful.

analyses.title: arXivEdits: Understanding the Human Revision Process in Scientific Writing
analyses.research_question: How can revisions across successive versions of full scientific papers be aligned, decomposed into fine-grained edits, and automatically classified by the authors' revision intentions?
analyses.methodology: The authors construct arXivEdits from 751 multi-version arXiv article groups containing 1,790 versions and manually annotate sentence alignment across 1,039 adjacent-version pairs, including 13,008 candidate sentence pairs. They additionally annotate fine-grained span edits and revision intentions for 1,000 sentence pairs using a seven-category intention taxonomy. Their automatic pipeline performs neural sentence alignment, span-alignment-based edit extraction, and edit-intention classification using models including semi-CRF alignment, QA-Align, PURE, and T5. Performance is measured with alignment F1, edit-extraction precision/recall/F1 and exact match, and intention-classification accuracy and weighted F1.

key_findings.finding: The corpus provides longitudinal full-document revision data for 751 papers and 1,790 versions, with manually annotated sentence alignment covering 13,008 sentence pairs.
The neural sentence-alignment model trained on arXivEdits achieved 93.8 F1, supporting automated linkage of corresponding sentences across document versions.
key_findings.section: Introduction; 4 Automatic Edit Extraction and Intention Identification

key_findings.finding: Span-alignment methods extracted finer-grained edits than latexdiff; QA-align with parse-based heuristics achieved 88.1 F1 on all revisions compared with 75.3 for latexdiff.

A T5-large intention classifier achieved 79.3 accuracy and 78.9 weighted F1 in the fine-grained eight-class experimental setup, while the collapsed four-class setup reached 84.4 accuracy and 84.6 weighted F1 when trained directly on four classes.
The annotated document-level alignments explicitly capture insertions, deletions, rephrasings, splits, merges, fusions, and unchanged copying across successive versions.

limitations: The corpus represents scientific-paper revision rather than workplace messages, tickets, incident reports, or operational work items.
Only 751 of 1,000 randomly selected multi-version article groups yielded complete usable plain text; groups without suitable LaTeX source or with overwhelming mathematical content were excluded.
The alignment procedure skips 5.8% of sentences that are too short or dominated by special tokens, although they remain marked in the dataset.
Fine-grained edit intentions are manually annotated for only 1,000 sentence pairs, much less than the full document-level corpus.
The intention taxonomy describes scientific-writing edits rather than explicit longitudinal operational relations such as supersession, supplementation, reopening, or work-item conflict.
The work does not distinguish an author's assertion that an external task has been completed from independently corroborating evidence of that completion.
raw_claims: arXivEdits follows adjacent versions of the same paper as longitudinal revisions.
The corpus contains 751 complete article groups and 1,790 paper versions.
Crowdworkers annotated sentence correspondence for 13,008 sentence pairs.
The fine-grained subset assigns intentions to span-level insertions, deletions, substitutions, and related edits.
The corpus defines seven semantic categories of revision intention.
Semantic span alignment produces substantially better fine-grained edit extraction than a conventional string-diff baseline.
T5-large is the strongest reported intention classifier in the evaluated configurations.
The released repository contains both data and pipeline code for revision analysis.

analyses.title: How and Why is An Answer (Still) Correct? Maintaining Provenance in Dynamic Knowledge Graphs
analyses.research_question: Can the validity and derivational provenance of standing-query answers over large knowledge graphs be maintained efficiently as underlying facts are inserted or deleted, rather than recomputed from scratch?
analyses.methodology: The authors introduce HUKA, which represents the how-provenance of each standing-query answer as a provenance polynomial whose monomials encode alternative sets of graph edges capable of deriving that answer. HUKA stores query results, one-edge-missing potential matches and subquery results, combines overlapping subplans into a global execution tree, and incrementally updates these structures after fact insertions or deletions. The system is evaluated in a single-threaded Java implementation over YAGO2 and DBpedia using SPARQL workloads and randomly generated insertion/deletion workloads, with GProM, ProvSQL, and Neo4j-based recomputation as baselines.

key_findings.finding: Provenance polynomials retain the individual graph facts and alternative derivations responsible for each query answer, allowing the system to explain both why an answer exists and how it was derived.
key_findings.section: 4 The HUKA Framework; 4.1 Why and How Provenance

key_findings.finding: After a fact deletion, an answer can remain valid when at least one provenance monomial still evaluates nonzero, so alternative derivations act as explicit independently surviving evidence paths.
Average update time was 0.119 seconds on YAGO2 and 1.252 seconds on DBpedia, and the authors report HUKA as roughly 4 to 48 times faster than the nearest compared baselines for update processing.
Combining common subquery work into a global execution plan reduced the number of intermediate expressions by close to 70%.
HUKA supports both insertion and deletion of graph facts and treats a factual update as a deletion followed by an insertion, enabling provenance to evolve with the underlying knowledge graph.
key_findings.section: 1.1 Contributions; 4 The HUKA Framework; 6 Update Processing

limitations: The method operates on structured knowledge graphs and SPARQL queries rather than natural-language workplace communication.
The query language is restricted to core basic graph-pattern conjunctive queries corresponding to select-project-join operations, with full SPARQL left for future work.
Path-expression queries are excluded because enumerating their derivational provenance can be intractable.
Evaluation updates are randomly generated graph insertions and deletions rather than naturally observed longitudinal revisions.

Provenance establishes which database facts derive an answer but does not itself classify natural-language semantic relations such as correction, supersession, supplementation, reopening, or conflict.
A surviving derivation demonstrates database-level support under the modeled facts, not the epistemic reliability or independence of the real-world sources that originally supplied those facts.
raw_claims: HUKA maintains provenance for answers to standing graph-pattern queries as the knowledge graph changes.
Each provenance monomial represents one derivation of a query answer through a particular combination of graph edges.
Multiple monomials can provide alternative derivations for the same answer.
Deleting one supporting fact does not invalidate an answer if another complete derivation remains.
The framework handles graph-fact insertions as well as deletions.
The experiments use YAGO2 and DBpedia with standing SPARQL query workloads.
The global execution tree reuses common computation among related subqueries.
The HUKA implementation is publicly available.

analyses.title: Belief Revision: The Adaptability of Large Language Models Reasoning
analyses.research_question: How reliably can language models decide whether a previously inferred conclusion should be updated or maintained when a new premise changes the conditions governing that conclusion?
analyses.methodology: The authors introduce the delta-reasoning framework, which evaluates a model at two consecutive stages: an initial two-premise inference at time t and a revised inference at time t+1 after adding a third premise. Belief-R is synthetically generated from ATOMIC with GPT-4-assisted construction and then human-annotated to determine whether the third premise creates an additional condition requiring a belief update or an alternative condition allowing the prior belief to be maintained. The dataset contains modus ponens and modus tollens cases, with separate Belief Update and Belief Maintain subsets. Roughly 30 language models are tested using zero-shot classification and, for larger generative models, direct, chain-of-thought, and plan-and-solve prompting, with BU-Acc, BM-Acc, and the balanced BREU measure reported.

key_findings.finding: Belief-R contains 1,912 basic two-premise cases and 1,744 three-premise revision cases, comprising 1,074 Belief Update and 670 Belief Maintain examples.

Models that perform well on the initial basic inference still perform poorly on belief revision; most non-API models have near-zero Belief Update accuracy, and the larger open and commercial models reach only about 50% at best on the balanced BREU measure.
The experiments reveal a trade-off between updating and maintaining prior conclusions, with models that improve on Belief Update often performing worse on Belief Maintain.
Belief revision is harder in the modus-tollens subset, where the models show lower balanced revision performance and a stronger imbalance between updating and maintaining.
Chain-of-thought prompting does not significantly improve average belief revision, and plan-and-solve prompting yields only about a one-percentage-point improvement in BREU overall.

The delta-reasoning formulation provides a direct sequential test of whether new evidence should revise or preserve a prior conclusion rather than evaluating reasoning only in a static information state.
key_findings.section: 3.2 Evaluating Belief Revision with Delta R

limitations: Belief-R focuses on modus ponens and modus tollens and therefore covers only a narrow subset of real-world revision phenomena.
Revision is primarily triggered by introduction of a new premise, not by reinterpretation of existing evidence without new information.
The paper operationalizes a model's belief as what it currently treats as true in context rather than measuring an internal cognitive state.
The authors note that measured reasoning performance can be entangled with the model's stored knowledge or recall ability.
The examples are synthetic commonsense reasoning scenarios derived from ATOMIC rather than observed workplace or operational communication.
The update-versus-maintain distinction does not separately label supersession, correction, supplementation, reopening, or conflict.
The framework does not distinguish a participant's claim of task completion from independent source evidence corroborating that completion.
raw_claims: Delta reasoning compares a model's conclusion before and after a new premise is introduced.
Belief-R explicitly separates cases where the old conclusion should be revised from cases where it should be retained.
The corpus contains 1,074 update cases and 670 maintain cases with three premises.
Human majority voting is used to establish the significance of the added premise and the target conclusion.
Strong performance on simple logical inference does not imply strong performance when evidence changes.
Models exhibit a measurable tension between sensitivity to updates and stability when no update is warranted.
Modus-tollens revision cases are more difficult than corresponding modus-ponens cases.
More elaborate zero-shot reasoning prompts provide little overall improvement in balanced belief-revision performance.
